turn_text: What were your biggest concerns when it came to making changes to Dodd-Frank? Were there any provisions that you felt really needed to be defended and really needed to be remained in the law?

Well, we knew that it would be really difficult if we were making changes in this bill for the largest institutions. And so very early on, I started talking to the largest banks saying, look, I know that there's some regulatory things that you would like to get done. But this is our top priority, which is getting regulatory relief for our small community banks and our regional banks. And I knew that it was probably a stretch to go to the regional bank area. But I felt strongly that that too big to fail had gotten worse because of the growth of the largest institutions and that if we were going to curb that problem, we needed to create a more competitive environment for the regional banks. Everybody, there was an agreement on the small institutions. There were some things like come to reform that I think some people would say there wasn't an agreement on, but I felt strongly because that increased paperwork would have such a devastating effect on lending in small organizations. And we're not promoting We're not promoting discrimination, but we are saying some of this doesn't really fit small institutions. And so when we go back and take a look at what we were able to do, we weren't able to do some fixes that I would have liked to have seen. Like, for instance, would be a single regulator for Volcker. I think that actually adds to accountability, but that wasn't something that could be put on this bill and generate the same level of support that we received. That's something that's going to have to stand alone. And I think everyone understood who's really been pushing for single regulator that that was something that couldn't be carried on this on this regional and small community bank bill.

Well, I thought we picked a line where most of the regional banks would fall under, not the super regionals. I think they felt a little left behind, but a lot of them are bumping up into that major category anyway. We thought it was an appropriate line drawing. And the important thing to know about the 250 is we did not eliminate the regulator's ability to bring them back in. So if they see systemic behavior that could create systemic risk in those smaller institutions. they can always bring them back in. It's a matter of opt-in or opt-out, and the Fed can bring them back in. So when we got the argument about country-wide, for instance, we would say, well, in an examination or a stress test, if you saw things that would make you concerned, you can bring them back in, but you're going to have to have a proof point to do it. The only thing we did was move the assumption. Is that anything below 50? No, it's anything below 250. We're not going to have the application.
